Ryan

messages.subject: Re: Open population analysis in secr?
messages.body_plain:
Open population models are a way to deal with this, but I'm not entirely convinced. Does Spacecap do open-population models? I hadn't caught up with that. 'secr' does not itself do open populations, but if you can wait 2-3 months there is other software in development that will fill that gap.

I suggest plowing on with a multi-session secr analysis: if the constant density estimated from a multi-session model is the same as density from a pooled single-session model then I think you can ignore turnover. CI from the multi-session model will be too short due to non-independence, so use those from the single-session model.  Or just relax: I suspect that your sample sizes are small enough that these minor analysis issues will be overwhelmed by sampling error.

Murray

messages.subject: Re: Open population analysis in secr?
messages.body_plain:
1. I would have said you could ignore the autoini warning, but you also have a problem with the g0 estimates themselves hitting the boundary at 1.0. (i) are you using a recent version of secr? (ii) for count data, especially, it makes sense to use one of the hazard-based detection functions (e.g. detectfn = 'HHN' not 'HN') for which the intercept is lambda0 not g0, (iii) I assume your traps object has non-null usage - be aware that will determine the scaling of g0 or lambda0. Your occasions in the single-session analysis seem to be about one month long, which is fine, but if you want a daily g0 or lambda0 then values in the usage matrix should be 30 rather than 1.
2. Density is expressed by 'secr' in animals per hectare. There are 100 hectares per sq km. 5 jaguar/100 km^2 seems alright to me - were you expecting more?
3. The SE of D-hat from the multi-session model is spuriously low because of non-independence as discussed before.
Non-closure seems like a non-issue, but you'll want to sort out the g0 issue before trusting the density estimates.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Not a stupid question, and there's not an obvious answer. I can only pick at the problem. I guess you were expecting something closer to 125 elephants? The number of 'recaptures' (potential re-locations) is effectively less than 29 - subtract one for the first capture of each of the 13 known individuals. The data include one elephant seen at least 7 times that may be distorting the results. Does the park have a natural boundary? If you buffered the park area when really no elephants come in from outside then the density estimate will be spuriously low. Life would be easier if you collapsed to fewer occasions (I can't remember if reduce() handles sightings properly, but it's worth a try).
Murray

Hi Lucas,
You might get different results between closure.test ('secr' package) and CAPTURE if your SECR data include additional recaptures (e.g. at different traps on the same occasion - not included in CR data).
Note that each of the closure tests have limitations.  I think it's the test of Stanley and Burnham that tends to reject if there is heterogeneity in capture probabilities among individuals - larger samples may increase the chance that this test will reject if there is heterogeneity (which there usually is).  The other test has low power to detect violation, but tends to reject in the presence of behavioural responses to detection... This is an incomplete description - best to look at the original references.

All the best,

1. secr.fit by default looks at your first session and constructs suitable starting values based on what it finds. If that fails, the details argument 'autoini' allows you to direct it to look at a different session. If that fails, you can specify actual starting values with something like start = list(D=1, g0=0.1, sigma=10). You should not be calling the autoini function.

2. I think you sort of understand what is going on but are expressing it, well, oddly. 'secr' does not estimate turnover per se (it does fit a model, just not that one). However, in 'secr' you can fit a model that treats each session as an independent unit of data; secr does this by maximising the sum of the session log-likelihoods. Yes, open populationSECR models have some appeal. For complete flexibility you will need to go to BUGS/JAGS or Ben Augustine's GitHub R package mentioned in a recent post, but a fairly functional maximum likelihood version will be available soon.

3. Good

4. OK, but I don't think you need to make the buffer uniform across species: better (or at least faster) to match it to the behaviour of each. Or are you throwing a lot of species into one analysis? I don't understand your point about trap days.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am running a secr analysis on captures of Tasmanian devils to compare the density and the home range size between three sessions (three different years with a known decrease in population size due to DFTD).

I am using the k parameter instead of sigma as described in Efford et al 2016 (in Ecography).

I have done a model selection which gives me the best model:

model                                     detectfn          npar  logLik      AIC         AICc        dAICc AICcwt

D~session lambda0~session sigmak~session  hazard halfnormal 9     -881.6317   1781.263      1783.028    0     0.6648

The results are:

                year1                     year2                     year3

D             0.00605                 0.00218                 0.00254

lambda 0.0508                   0.0475                   0.0272

k              125.09                   102.72                   102.54

sigma    1608                       2200                       2034

The densities are pretty good estimates and reflects the trapping observations.

My question is relative to the interpretation of the k and sigma parameters:

Based on sigma, the home range size is bigger in year 2 and 3 than year 1.
That is the opposite of the tracking data, which shows a decrease in HR size with a decrease in overlap.

I have looked at the model with a constant k over the years (sigmak~1), but the result is similar.

Devils are solitary non-territorial animals so I am not sure the secr model reflects the ecology of the species.

Does anyone have some experience with secr and non-territorial species?

The other issue is that while the density decreased over time, the resources didn’t change.

This is the main hypothesis explaining the decrease in HR size and overlap observed with the tracking data.

Would that be an issue for the secr?

Thank you for any information you have regarding the interpretation of the data.

Hi Sebastien
I think you probably have as clear an idea of this as anyone, but here's my 2 cents worth anyway.

1. The trapping data broadly suggest an increase in home range size with a decrease in density, as expected - it's only when you zoom in that particular differences seem odd, and maybe that is overinterpreting.
2. Constant-k is an interesting benchmark, but there is no law here. Transient deviations might be especially interesting (there was some hand waving on this for tigers in the Ecography paper) and DFTD may be one such.
3. If the telemetry data conflict it's not necessarily the trapping results that are wrong! I'm assuming only a selection of animals were telemetered...
4. You have reported the sigmak produced by 'secr', but for comparative purposes really it's good to divide by 100 (allowing for the different units for area and length in secr).
5. There are many estimates of sigma and density for brushtail possums (another nonterritorial marsupial). k tends to fall in the range you have for devils - somewhat more overlap than territorial species I've looked at, but not totally out of range. I'll send some unpublished data offline.

Cheers
Murray

I am hoping to use SECR to analyze a large historical dataset of live captures (~2400 total captures, ~580 traps (with varying effort), 850 occasions). I have some questions regarding how to set up my models.

1) The data were collected over multiple years, so I am planning to use multi-session models to meet the closure assumption. I understand that sessions are intended to be independent, but I am struggling with how to define the length of the sessions to best meet that assumption. Of course changing session length alters the number of recaptures in a session. How much does session length and the number of recaptures within a session matter if I am interested in a single estimate of density rather than session-specific estimates? Does having sessions of varying length bias estimates?

In this study, around 30 traps at a time were generally set for 2 week blocks. Thus there is often some proportion of traps >0% but <100% that were trapped in the previous week, which seems to make it difficult to decide where one session should end and another should begin. Below is a figure showing distances moved, excluding those of 0/recaptures at the same trap to make it easier to see the outliers. The study area here is not geographically constrained like on a small island, aside from a river on one side. Is sigma going to be skewed by these long movements?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura
Big questions - this is the most critical stage of any analysis! I assume from other clues that your traps were not really traps, but rather some sort of proximity detector (DNA hair snag, camera?). That gives you more freedom to aggregate data, particularly by collapsing occasions using outputdetector 'count' in reduce.capthist. (reduce(CH, ...). Aggregation makes the problem solvable (580 occasions is too many) without sacrificing anything (except possibly the ability to model day to day variation in detection , but who cares about that?).

1. Short session length does not cause bias, but it reduces the number of recaptures (because recaptures between sessions don't count) and hence reduces the precision of estimates of lambda0 and sigma. That may or may not be critical in your case - it depends on the data.

I assume you specify 'usage' to allow for detectors used/not used on particular occasions. Can't really advise on specifics as they depend on the pattern of use/non-use. If your traps are not really traps then you have a lot more latitude, and can even define notional occasions (secondary sessions) that are asynchronous in real time (Efford Borchers & Mowat 2013 MEE).

2. "long-tailed detection function will better fit the data, but these are not really advised" I guess I am partly responsible for that advice. The worry about long tails is that they potentially make the density estimates dependent on the extent of the habitat mask. You have to be aware of that; it may be inescapable. I have relaxed a bit myself and started using long-tailed detection functions to accommodate occasional extreme movements - may be the lesser of two risks. Can assess impact with your own data. Long movements will result in the fitting of a halfnormal function with larger sigma than if the movements didn't happen, sure; probably that will bias density estimates low, but I doubt it's a big effect in your case. See the usual advice about buffers and habitat masks (secr-habitatmasks.pdf). <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-habitatmasks.pdf>

Murray

messages.subject: secrlinear and usage
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm using the secrlinear package to look at density of our study species in streams. We did not visit each trap on every occasion, so I added usage information to the capture history object with 0/1 data to indicate which traps were visited on each occasion. This information appears to have read in correctly, because the capture history summary lists the correct number of traps visited in the 'detectors used' row. However, our detection probabilities are much lower than expected and much lower than when the data were analyzed with other approaches (i.e. regular capture-recapture methods with no spatial information). Is it possible that the usage information is not being taken into account when fitting the model? If not, how is the interpretation of g0 different from a typical detection probability, and is it reasonable to see substantially lower values?

Here's my rationale for thinking that usage may be the problem: Our fitted g0 values were around 0.01-0.03. We had 81 total occasions, with each trap visited on 16 of those occasions. We had 117 marked individuals seen during our study, with 325 total detections across the 16 occasions. Therefore, we observed 325 detections out of 1872 possible detections (117 individuals × 16 occasions = 1872 total possible detections), which would roughly result in a detection probability of 0.17. If usage is not being accounted for, then the 325 detections is out of 9477 possible detections (117 individuals × 81 occasions = 9477 total possible detections), which results in a detection probability of 0.03, as in the fitted results. I don't know what else goes into g0, but a detection probability of 0.03 seems very low given our number of detections relative to our number of occasions.

Is there anything I should be doing differently? Or any suggestions for understanding and interpreting g0?

Thank you,
Wendy

Here's the code for adding usage information, with traps_m as a data frame with 81 columns and 0/1 values:
usage(traps(RegCH)) <- traps_m[,start:end]

I attached most of the summary(RegCH) in a word document

Here is an example of my code to run a model:
Reg <- secr.fit(RegCH,
                     model = list(D ~ Location,
                                  g0 ~ h2,
                                  sigma ~ h2),
                     mask = streammask,
                     hcov = 'Sex',
                     details = list(userdist = distmat),

Let me know if any additional information would be helpful.

messages.subject: Re: secrlinear and usage
messages.body_plain:
Hi Wendy,

Unlike p in non-spatial CR models, g0 is both trap- and occasion-specific. It's the probability that an animal with a trap placed at it's activity center (i.e. at distance 0 from it's activity center) will be detected at that trap, on one occasion. Adding traps does not increase g0.  Non-spatial probability of detection (p in CR models) is the probability of detecting an animal at any trap (i.e., at the entire array of traps) on an occasion, so it's higher than g0, and adding traps increases p.

Also, if the duration of an occasion is short, g0 will be small (less opportunity detect animals during each occasion).

The same is true if the traps are not very effective at detecting animals in their vicinity (so tends to increase e.g. when traps are baited).

Good luck,
Eric

Hello Bruna

I think your data need to be simplified in various ways to become manageable.

1. The mask you provide has been built with a buffer much larger than needed given the apparently small scale of movements - 2000 m would be plenty. The mask can be made much smaller and more manageable by setting keep.poly = FALSE in make.mask (or retrospectively setting to NULL for each mask in the list).

2. You have an enormous number of detectors (what were they? what were the trap types?) and the 'usage' matrix I looked at was very sparse, so I'm suspicious there.

3. You have only a few dozen recaptures overall, so there's probably no need for sophistication in the  detection model. With many (daily?) samples the model will take forever to fit, so I would consider collapsing to one occasion (but I was unsure what was safe because i don't understand the detectors).

4. I haven't seen that 'contrasts' message before - was it really an error or just a warning? It is something I need to check further. However, I think you do not need to be specifying that details option, certainly not until you have everything else sorted.

5. "length(start) == NP is not TRUE" just means your start vector is wrong; it's safer to use the form start = list (D= , g0 =, sigma = ) because then you don't need to provide all beta parameters, not all real parameters if you don't want.

Cheers

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running into two problems while attempting to add telemetry data to a hair snare trapping dataset. The hair snare dataset has 1 session, 8 occasions, 36 detectors, 41 individuals detected a total of 77 times. The concurrent telemetry dataset includes 11 telemetered individuals, 8 of which were detected on hair snares, with 329-5149 locations per animal (app. 26,000 points total). Telem data were collapsed to a single session.

My two problems are:
1) On using addTelemetry, I get a warning that the covariates in the telemetry CH do not match the detection CH. The detection CH included sex covariates. I attempted to add a 'sex' column (M/F) to the telemetry txt file but got the same error. Is there a way to include sex covariates and telem data? I have not found documentation on this.

#In addTelemetry(HSjanapr17, HStelem17, type = c("concurrent"), #collapsetelemetry = TRUE,  :
  #covariates in telemetryCH do not match detectionCH so covariates discarded

If I move forward anyway, I run into:
2) A returned likelihood NA when I call secr.fit. In line with suggestions from the 'Telemetry data in secr 3.0' vignette, I have tried triple checking the telem file for location errors, changing the detection function to HEX, scaling telemetry data between 1e3 to 1e12, and including trace=TRUE and details = list(debug=1) .... none of which have budged it. Initial  values for D, g0, and sigma seem reasonable to me.
It appears that the problems start from the beginning:

#Initial values  D = 0.00232, g0 = 0.13603, sigma = 1159.68168

#Likelihood components 9.3464 -398.7629 0 0 0 0
 #  1         NA  -1.9226   7.0559
.....
Warning messages:
1: In FUN(X[[i]], ...) :
  zero likelihood with telemetry data suggests numerical problem - try larger telemetryscale

Thanks in advance for any and all help in navigating these problems!
Below are relevant code and the three input files, if helpful in diagnosing.

Darcy

HSjanapr17 <- read.capthist("hs_janapr17_caps.txt", "hs_janapr17_traps.txt", detector = "multi", covnames = "sex")

HSMask <- make.mask(traps(HSjanapr17), buffer = 10000, spacing=500, type = c("trapbuffer"), poly = nonHab, poly.habitat = FALSE)

HStelem17<-read.telemetry(file = "telemdataHS172.txt")

HSjanapr17telem<-addTelemetry(HSjanapr17, HStelem17, type= c("concurrent"), collapsetelemetry =TRUE, verify=TRUE)

HS17fit1<-secr.fit(HSjanapr17telem, mask = HSMask, detectfn = 'HHN', CL=TRUE, details = list(debug = 1), trace = TRUE)

--
Darcy Doran-Myers
University of Alberta
Biological Sciences- Ecology

Murray

messages.subject: Model average
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

I am interested in estimating population change over time and I have mark-recapture data for several years. I have fit three models using D~ 1, D~session, D~Session where the Sessions are the years. The null model (D~1) estimates density as a constant across years, the second model D~session estimates density for each year independently, and the last model indicates a trend across sessions where the beta value is r or the rate of exponential growth.

The top two models are D~1 and D~Session and both have similar AIC weights and D~session is not supported. I understand how to calculate a model averaged estimate of r (the beta value for D.Session) however I am uncertain how to estimate the standard error of the model averaged r.

Any help is appreciated.

Michelle
